tagline: A gravel loop follows older journeys across the Continental Divide.
intro: The Lewis and Clark Back Country Byway makes a 36-mile loop from Tendoy through river valley, sagebrush grasslands, mountain forests and high desert canyons. This single-lane gravel road has pullouts, steep exposed slopes without guardrails and grades approaching 20 percent. The Bureau of Land Management presents it as a journey through scenery and history on the Lewis and Clark National Historic Trail and Continental Divide National Scenic Trail. The loop gains and loses 4,000 feet in elevation, and the agency guide calls for at least three hours to drive it.

The expedition followed established trails in the homeland of the Agai Dika Shoshone, later known as the Lemhi Shoshone. After the railroad reached Dillon in 1880, Salmon residents pooled resources to build a road over the pass to Red Rock’s rail station. Stage service began in the late 1880s and lasted until the railway reached Salmon over Bannock Pass in 1910.

Drive clockwise from Tendoy along the Lemhi back road, then climb Warm Springs Wood Road into the Beaverhead Mountains. Past the Flag Unfurling Monument and Pattee Creek Overlook, the road turns south near the Continental Divide toward Lemhi Pass. Agency Creek Road returns to Tendoy, passing Horseshoe Bend Creek below the pass.

moments.title: Flag Unfurling Monument
moments.text: Lewis had set out to find the Shoshone because he hoped their horses could carry the expedition’s baggage over the divide. The monument marks Lewis’s advance party displaying the United States flag on August 13, 1805, the first such display in present-day Idaho. Earlier contact that day began when the four explorers encountered three Shoshone women. Lewis gave them gifts and persuaded them to lead his party toward their encampment. On the way, they met Chief Cameahwait and sixty warriors. When the women showed Cameahwait the gifts, he welcomed the strangers as friends.

moments.title: Lemhi Pass
moments.text: The Shoshones called this crossing We-yah-vee and used it for generations before Lewis and Clark arrived. On August 12, 1805, Lewis reached the divide and recorded more mountain ranges to the west, their tops partly covered in snow. Later travelers crossed by stagecoach: eight dollars bought a one-way, twelve-hour trip from Salmon to Red Rock. The pass itself owes its low saddle to a fault zone, where fractured rock erodes faster than the surrounding rock. Stations supplied meals and replacement horses and mules; the stage company operated as many as fourteen coaches and twelve freight wagons.

moments.title: Horseshoe Bend Creek
moments.text: Lewis and his men drank where Horseshoe Bend Creek joins Agency Creek, 0.4 mile below the sharp road curve. After seeing the mountains beyond Lemhi Pass, they took comfort in believing this water would eventually reach the Columbia River. Agency Creek rises west of Lemhi Pass and flows to the Lemhi River at Tendoy.

practical: Lemhi Pass: Allow at least three hours. Agency Creek Road is not suitable for trailers, buses or motorhomes. The byway is normally snow-free from early June through October. (checked 2026-10-11)
